newsitem.title: USA: Clinton preferred over Dole on issues - Reuter poll.
newsitem.headline: Clinton preferred over Dole on issues - Reuter poll.

text.p: Voters give President Bill Clinton higher marks than Bob Dole on virtually every major campaign issue, and Clinton's support increased after he took action against Iraq, a Reuters poll said on Thursday.

The poll, conducted for Reuters by John Zogby International, showed Clinton's public support went up on campaign issues ranging from taxes, to drugs and foreign policy after he ordered missile strikes against Iraq.
Of the 12 campaign issues surveyed, voters said Clinton was better able to handle 10 of them. Dole was preferred over Clinton only on the issues of foreign policy and character.
"As the planes and missiles soared (in Iraq), so did the public view of Clinton on every aspect," Zogby told Reuters.
"There is a likeability factor here. Clinton acted decisively, and that enhanced his favourability. It lifted him on all the issues," Zogby said.

The poll of 1019 likely voters taken Monday evening through Wednesday evening found Democrat Clinton leading his Republican challenger Dole overall by 48.2 percent to 33.3 percent, with 5.9 percent selecting Reform candidate Ross Perot.

When voters were asked about specific issues, they considered Clinton better than Dole at handling education (55 to 25 percent), the environment (51 percent to 19 percent), health care (49 percent to 28 percent), the economy (47 percent to 28 percent), tobacco (46 percent to 21 percent), abortion (42 percent to 28 percent) the deficit (38 to 31 percent) and crime (38 percent to 34 percent).
Clinton did especially well on the issues identified by voters in a Reuters poll last month as the most important -- education and the economy.

Even on taxes and drugs, the themes Dole has emphasised in his recent campaigning, Americans prefer Clinton slightly, the poll said. But Zogby said Dole scored better on his handling of both of those subjects until Clinton moved against Iraq.

Dole had an eight-point lead on his handling of the tax issue in the early polling Monday evening, 39 to 31 percent, Zogby said. By the time the poll finished, voters were saying they favoured Clinton slightly on taxes, 37 percent to 33 percent.
Something similar happened with the drug issue, with Dole leading Clinton at first by 33 to 30 percent on Monday but Clinton finishing ahead at the end, 34 percent to Dole's 32 percent.
And on the two issues in which Dole did beat Clinton in the poll -- foreign policy and character -- Dole's lead narrowed after the president's decisions on Iraq.
Among the first 304 people polled Monday, Dole led Clinton on foreign policy by 44 to 32 percent and on character by a whopping 51 to 23 percent.

But by the time the polling finished Wednesday, Dole's lead on foreign policy had narrowed to 42 percent to Clinton's 35 percent. On character Dole's earlier 28-point lead also had eroded, leaving him with 45 percent to Clinton's 28 percent.

Zogby said the findings indicated it would be very hard for Dole to pull ahead of Clinton by emphasising any one issue, even taxes. Dole has sought to sell voters on a proposal for a 15 percent across-the-board cut in tax rates.
"In and of itself it (the tax issue) is not going to be enough, because Dole is behind on so much else," Zogby said.
He said Dole needs some dramatic outside event, not unlike Clinton's opportunity in Iraq, to give him a boost with the public.

"Clearly the voters are not listening to Dole. He has not bonded. He needs an outside force, perhaps something out of his control, like a Whitewater indictment against someone really high up, or a foreign policy conflagration like something awful in Bosnia," Zogby said.
